lesson.title: One Promoter, One Decision, Many Genes: The Operon
lesson.summary: An operon is a cluster of bacterial genes, usually encoding proteins that work together in one pathway, transcribed as a single mRNA from one promoter and switched on or off as a single unit.
lesson.body:
Bacteria frequently need several different enzymes at once, for instance every enzyme required to break down a particular sugar, or every enzyme required to build a particular amino acid. Rather than giving each of those genes its own separate promoter and its own separate regulatory switch, bacteria commonly arrange such genes together into an operon: a set of structural genes, physically adjacent to one another on the chromosome, that share a single promoter and are transcribed together into one continuous mRNA molecule.

Because that single mRNA carries the coding sequences for multiple proteins, one after another, it is called a polycistronic mRNA, and bacterial ribosomes are able to initiate translation independently at the start codon of each gene within it, producing several separate proteins from one transcript. This is different from how most eukaryotic genes work, where each gene typically has its own promoter and is transcribed into its own separate, monocistronic mRNA, a distinction that becomes relevant again later in this unit.

An operon typically includes a promoter, the DNA sequence where RNA polymerase binds to begin transcription, and an operator, a regulatory DNA sequence usually overlapping or sitting just next to the promoter, where a repressor protein can bind to physically block RNA polymerase. The regulatory protein that controls the operon, whether a repressor or an activator, is usually encoded by a separate regulatory gene with its own promoter, expressed independently of the operon it controls.

The advantage of this arrangement is coordination and economy. A single regulatory event, one repressor releasing one operator, or one activator binding one site, switches transcription of every gene in the operon on or off together, ensuring that a full, matched set of enzymes for one pathway is produced, or not produced, as a coordinated unit rather than as a patchwork of independently timed genes. The next two chapters examine the two most thoroughly studied operons in biology, the lac operon and the trp operon, which illustrate the two opposite logical strategies, negative control paired with induction, and negative control paired with repression, that bacteria use to decide when a pathway's genes should be on.
